title: Domestication of wheat and barley
summary: Cereal farming arose in the Fertile Crescent of southwestern Asia. Barley remains show almost purely wild, shattering plants before 9500 BC, then non-shattering ears rising to as much as 30% in a few sites between 9000 and 8500 BC, and fixed at some sites after 7400 BC. The earliest domesticated barley samples come from Jarmo in northern Iraq. Bread wheat later became a staple food of humanity.

uncertainty.note: Chronology spans the Pre-Pottery Neolithic transition from wild cereal gathering before 9500 BC to peak selection and fixation of non-shattering rachides between 8500 and 7500 BC.

as_recorded.value: almost purely wild-type, fully shattering populations before 9500 BC, with the gradual appearance of non-shattering rachides, rising to as much as 30% in a few assemblages, between 9000 and 8500 BC
between 9,500 and 8,500 years BP for tetraploid and hexaploid wheat
The domestication of barley occurred between 8,400 and 9,500 years ago
After 7400 BC some sites show apparently fixed, 100% non-shattering barley

where.modern_name: Fertile Crescent; stand-in pin at Çayönü, Turkey
where.historical_name: Tigris-Euphrates headwaters, northern Fertile Crescent, Pre-Pottery Neolithic; no polities existed

importance.justification: The agricultural revolution's foundational breakthrough, establishing cereal grain staples that sustained sedentary human settlement, state formation, and world civilization.

related.because: The package of domesticated wheat, barley, and sheep-goat husbandry spread from the Fertile Crescent across southeastern and central Europe.
Surplus grain production from domesticated emmer and barley irrigation agriculture made permanent urban density and state taxation possible.
